words.etymon: unmapped (context-after line of the cited passage; = *h₂eh₃mó- 'raw' + *h₁ed- 'eat')

cognate: Gk ὠμός = Ved. āmá- (*h₂eh₃mó- 'raw'); Gk κρέας = Ved. kravís- (*kréwh₂s 'raw flesh'); Gk ἔδ-/ἐσθ- = Ved. ad- (*h₁ed- 'eat'); nominal compound Gk ὠμ-ηστής 'raw-eater' = Ved. āma-ád- 'raw-eater' (RV 10.87.7), with the parallel Ved. kravy-ád- 'flesh-eater' built on the cognate of κρέας.
drift_or_renewal: AVŚ 8.6.48 renews 'flesh' with māṃsa- (āmaṃ māṃsam adanti) beside kraviḥ in the same line; Greek κρέας has generalised to 'meat' and needs ὠμά to keep the 'raw' sense; Greek -ηστής is a new agent formation on *h₁ed- where Vedic keeps the root noun -ád-.
shared_syntax: Phrase: object 'raw flesh' (adjective *h₂eh₃mó- + noun *kréwh₂s) governed by *h₁ed- 'eat' (Il. 22.347 ὤμ' ... κρέα ἔδμεναι; AVŚ 8.6.48 āmaṃ māṃsam adanti ... kraviḥ; Hdt. κρεῶν ἐδεσταὶ ὠμῶν); the same three-way relation compressed into an agentive compound adjective/noun *h₂eh₃mo-h₁ed- (ὠμηστής ~ āmā́d-).
context: Both traditions use the epithet of carrion-eaters that devour the unburied body of a slain enemy: Homer of dogs and birds that tear the corpse (Il. 22.66-67 κύνες ... ὠμησταὶ ἐρύουσιν; Il. 11.454 οἰωνοὶ ὠμησταί), Vedic of the creatures and demons that eat raw/human flesh, prayed against or set upon the enemy (RV 10.87.7 āmā́daḥ kṣviṅkā́s tam adantu; AVŚ 8.6.48 'who eat raw flesh, human flesh'; AVŚ 8.4.4 the kravyā́d hated by Indra-Soma). Achilles' wish to eat Hector raw (Il. 22.347) shows the same phrase as a curse of utmost savagery. The congruence is not just the three ordinary words: it is the same compound type, the same pejorative/curse register and the same scene type (bodies of enemies given to raw-eaters).
phrase: *h₂eh₃mo-h₁ed- 'raw-eater' / *h₂eh₃móm kréwh₂s h₁ed- 'eat raw flesh' (ὠμηστής ~ āmā́d-; ὠμὰ κρέα ἔδμεναι ~ āmaṃ ... kraviḥ adanti)

cognate: Gk ὄφις/ἔχις = Ved. áhi- (*h₁ógʷʰis 'snake'); Gk γῆρας 'old age' = Ved. jūrṇá-/jīrṇá- 'aged, worn out' (*ǵerh₂- 'grow old'), both used for the snake's cast skin.
drift_or_renewal: Greek has nominalised the 'age' word into the technical/folk name of the slough itself (Aristotle: τὸ καλούμενον γῆρας 'the so-called old age'), whereas Vedic keeps the participle as attribute of an explicit 'skin' noun (jūrṇā́ tvác-, later jīrṇā tvac-). The verb of the action is renewed in each: Gk ἐκ-δύ- 'strip off (a garment)', Ved. áti sr̥p- 'creep out of', later nir-muc- / hā- 'release, leave'. Latin (Lucretius) keeps the garment figure with non-cognate uestis and exuo (and, from memory outside this corpus, Latin senectus/senecta 'slough' is a calque-like renewal of the 'old age' noun with *sen-).
shared_syntax: Subject 'snake' (*h₁ógʷʰis) + verb of leaving/stripping + object (or ablative) 'the old one' (*ǵerh₂- derivative), the slough being called 'old (age)'.
context: Same natural-history scene in both: the snake casting its old skin. In the RV it is a simile for Soma passing out of its old 'skin' (the filter) renewed; in later Vedic prose it is the stock simile for shedding sin and renewal (yathā́hiḥ ... jīrṇāyās tvaco nirmucyeta); in Greek it is the standard word for the slough (Aristotle, repeatedly) and in Aristophanes a figure of rejuvenation (τὸ γῆρας ἐκδύς). What is shared beyond the observation is the lexical choice: both name the cast skin with the inherited 'grow old' root, so that 'shedding old age' = rejuvenation is built into the idiom in both branches. Weaknesses: 'old skin' is a natural phrase and could arise independently, and the verbs are not cognate.
phrase: *h₁ógʷʰis ... *ǵerh₂- 'the snake (sheds) its old age/old skin' (ὄφεις ἐκδύνουσι τὸ γῆρας ~ áhir ná jūrṇā́m áti sarpati tvácam)

note: Slab dominated by Aristotle biology/physics pivots with automatic partners; almost all bundles share only common roots. Two claims (raw-eater/raw flesh; snake sheds 'old age'). Considered and rejected: pitch on cattle horns (Arist. HA ~ Cato Agr. 72; shared Mediterranean veterinary lore, non-cognate verbs), 'sweeter than honey' (μέλι/mel + γλυκύς/dulcis cognate but referent-driven and universal; Vedic renews both), sleep/wake merism (*swep-/*h₁ger-; generic, contexts incongruent), sinews+bones (generic anatomy). Note: HA 8.26 s9 ὤμους (shoulders) is mis-mapped to h₂eh₃mós.
